turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. How are you keeping?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I'm not the worst, doctor. The wife is out in the waiting room, she drove, though we sat in the rain a fair while finding a parking spot.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): She's welcome in if she wants later. What brought you in today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this left hand. Since the stroke it's still a small bit weak, and I wanted you to see it now it's three months on.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about that hand, in your own words.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The grip is down, I can hold a cup of tea but the fingers won't close right, and the shirt buttons in the morning are a pure nightmare. It's there all the time, a slight weakness, and I'm right-handed so I manage most things. The wife still has to do the jars for me.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): The stroke itself, how long ago was that?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months. They kept me in, said it was a mild one down the left side, and I was talking away in the hospital before I came home on the tablets.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's the walking been?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Walking, well, I do get out, the wife links me as far as the shop and then we...
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're grand, finish that thought.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Since the stroke, these three months, I can walk but I'm slower than I was, and the left foot doesn't lift right. It scuffs the path if I'm tired. I don't use a stick.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the speech, is that back to itself?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah the speech is grand, not a bother at all. Everyone understands me no problem.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on now?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): All by mouth. The asprin is seventy-five milligrams every morning with breakfast, to thin the blood, and I've had that the three months since I came home. The atorvastin is 40 mg at night for the cholesterol, the same three months. And an amlodopine, sorry, amlodipine, five milligrams once a day in the morning for the pressure, about five years now.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's have a look at the pressure, arm out nice and relaxed.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): It'll read high, I get nervous in here. Last time it was better, one-thirty something, I can't remember the exact figure.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Today it's one hundred and fifty-eight over ninety-two. A bit higher than I'd like after a stroke.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I did take the five milligram tablet this morning, with the tea, so it's not that I forgot it.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know you didn't. Any pain in the chest?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): The chest, umm, we were up the hill with the dog yesterday and he was pulling like mad and I thought...
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did the chest hurt you on the hill?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain, not on the hill and not any other time.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the eyes, any blurring or seeing double?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the eyes are fine. I got reading glasses off the chemist last year, but that's only for small print, just age.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are the waterworks, any trouble passing water?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no trouble at all there.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to tablets, or to anything else?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No allergies that I know of, and I've never come out in a rash from a tablet.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the family, anyone with sugar or the pressure or a stroke?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh there's a good few of us, my father had diabetes in his fifties, on tablets for years. My mother did not, she never had the sugar or the pressure, and she lived to eighty-eight. My older brother had a stroke of his own at sixty-two, a bigger one than mine. And another sister has the pressure but no sugar, she's down in Cork and well able.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a help, thank you. What about your own days, the work, the food, exercise, a drink?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah now, where do I even start with all that, it's been a long old...
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wherever you like, I'm listening.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I was a postman thirty-seven years and I retired two years ago, though I still go in. Tuesdays and Thursdays I sort for four hours, half eight till half twelve. The diet is porridge through the week and a fry on a Sunday, rashers and egg, and I walk the dog most evenings, about twenty minutes round the green. I'll take a pint of Guinness on a Friday, sometimes a second if the match is on, and I never smoked a day in my life.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lovely, that gives me the picture. May I examine the hand?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): You may. They're a bit cold off the rain, and this wedding ring is stuck fast, which is a whole other story the wife won't let drop.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): The grip is a little weaker on the left than the right. You get the arm all the way up, there's no droop in the face, and the left foot scuffed a small bit when you walked in.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): The face was the bit that frightened the wife at the time, it was pulled down on the left, but that's gone, thank God, completely gone. She still watches me at the dinner to be sure.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good that the face cleared. Is there anything you haven't told me?

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Well actually, the speech, I said it was grand and that isn't the full of it. I lose the odd word, a thing's name or a person's, gone a second and then it comes back. I couldn't put a date on when it first started, somewhere around the stroke, I just can't say. It frightens me a small bit when it happens.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is that happening?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): A few times a week, not every day. It's not slurred at all, people follow me, it just takes a second to find the word.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Searching for words can linger after a mild stroke, and I'd say that's the size of it, the hand, the foot and the words left over from it, with the pressure still a bit high. I don't think this is a fresh stroke.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So what are we doing about the pressure, then?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll stop the five milligram amlodipine and start ten milligrams, once every morning, by mouth, for the pressure. Stand up slow from the chair, and if you get light-headed, sit down and ring the surgery.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten, grand. I keep the asprin and the night tablet as they are?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): You do, no change to those two. The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, a fasting cholesterol and the kidney function.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday morning. Am I fasting for that, and what about the tablets that day?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing to eat or drink except water from midnight, take the asprin and the new amlodipine with a sip of water, and leave the atorvastin until after the bloods. If those results are borderline we do a third test, the liver bloods, and if the weakness in the hand does not settle, a scan, but I'm not booking a scan now.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So the liver test and the scan are only if. I can do Thursday, I'm not in the depot that morning.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Exactly, only if. I'll see you back here in two weeks with the results, whatever they show. Keep those evening walks going, and maybe leave the Friday drink at the one pint.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, one pint, Thursday bloods. Thanks a million, doctor, I'll collect the wife on the way out.

spec.situation: Patient three months after a mild stroke with a spouse; slight weakness in the left hand; takes aspirin, atorvastatin and an amlodipine tablet; blood pressure read aloud; walking and speech discussed.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Same blood draw is not stated in the transcript.
bad.text: Kidney function blood test on Thursday morning from the same blood draw (action_type=investigation, status=planned, responsible_person=doctor)

omissions.text: Left hand weakness details not captured: reduced grip, fingers will not close properly, difficulty buttoning shirts, can still hold a cup of tea, and wife has to open jars.
Patient said he does not use a stick despite slower walking/left foot problems.
Speech was initially recorded by the patient as back to normal/no bother and everyone understands him, before he later clarified intermittent word-finding difficulty.
Patient reported he took his amlodipine 5 mg that morning and had not forgotten it.
Family history negative detail omitted: mother never had diabetes or high blood pressure and lived to age 88.
Examination detail omitted: hands were cold from the rain (patient comment).
